c.tagline: Colombia's oldest surviving city — Caribbean beaches, Sierra Nevada peaks, and the gateway to Tayrona and the Lost City.

taxi.fareNote: Santa Marta taxis are largely unmetered; agree the fare before getting in, or use an app that quotes the price up front.

emergency.note: 123 is Colombia's unified nationwide emergency line for police, fire, and ambulance.

avoid.reason: Caution around the market and away from the tourist centre at night

hood_desc: The 500-year-old colonial core around the cathedral and the seafront Camellón, with pastel streets, rooftop bars, boutique hotels, and the city's best nightlife and dining; the most atmospheric base.
Santa Marta's main resort beach a short drive south, a horseshoe bay lined with high-rise hotels, seafood restaurants, an aquarium, and boat departures to nearby coves; lively and family-friendly.
A former fishing village turned bohemian backpacker hangout over the headland, with a rugged bay, cheap hostels, dive shops, and boats to Playa Grande; laid-back and gritty.
A quieter residential and vacation-apartment strip of beach between Rodadero and Pozos Colorados, calmer than the resort centers and popular with families renting condos.
A stretch of resort hotels and long beaches south of the city near the airport, all-inclusive in feel and removed from the city bustle; best for a relaxed sun-and-sand stay.

water.note: Unlike Bogotá, tap water here is unreliable — stick to bottled or filtered.

transit.hours: City buses and busetas run roughly 5:00 AM to 10:00 PM; taxis and ride apps cover late nights.
transit.note: Santa Marta has no metro or rail; getting around means local buses and busetas, cheap taxis, and walking the compact Centro, with taxis or apps for trips out to Rodadero and Taganga.
transit.pay: Bus fares are paid in cash to the driver; there is no rechargeable transit card. Taxi fares are negotiated or app-quoted rather than metered.

landmarks: Parque Nacional Natural Tayrona
Jungle trails open onto boulder-strewn Caribbean coves like Cabo San Juan, making this coastal park Colombia's most celebrated natural treasure.
Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino
The gracious sugar hacienda where Simón Bolívar died in 1830, now a shrine of gardens, museums and monumental memorials to the Liberator.
Catedral Basílica de Santa Marta
Gleaming white and begun in 1766, one of Latin America's oldest cathedrals briefly held Bolívar's remains and anchors the historic centre.
Parque de los Novios
The restored colonial 'Lovers' Park' is Santa Marta's nightlife heart, ringed by restaurant terraces beneath strings of festive lights.
Museo del Oro Tairona (Casa de la Aduana)
In the customs house where Bolívar lay in state, glittering Tairona goldwork introduces the indigenous civilisations of the Sierra Nevada.
Taganga
A horseshoe fishing bay turned laid-back diving hub, where cliffside paths deliver famous sunsets over bobbing wooden boats.
Playa El Rodadero
Santa Marta's lively resort beach south of the centre, its calm waters backed by high-rises, seafood kiosks and boat touts.
Playa Cristal
A protected Tayrona-area cove with visitor limits, whose transparent turquoise shallows offer the region's easiest first-class snorkelling.
Camellón Rodrigo de Bastidas
The seafront promenade of South America's oldest surviving city, tracing the bay past the marina to statues of its Tairona and Spanish founders.
Parque de Bolívar
The city's oldest square, laid out by Spanish colonists and centered on a bronze statue of Simón Bolívar mounting his horse.

train.note: Colombia has no intercity passenger rail - the line through Santa Marta carries coal to the port and nothing else. Travel is by coach or by air into Simón Bolívar airport, about 20 minutes from the centre.

intl.to: Maracaibo (Venezuela) - via the Paraguachón border, status varies

bus.note: The Venezuela route runs when the border is open, which has fluctuated in recent years - check the current position and your visa situation before planning around it. Domestic coaches from the Santa Marta terminal reach Cartagena in about 4 hours, Barranquilla in 2 and Bogotá overnight in 16-18, on Expreso Brasilia and Copetran; book through Pinbus (https://pinbus.com/). Minibuses and vans serve Taganga, Palomino and the Tayrona park entrances.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry from Santa Marta - the port is a coal and cruise terminal. Boats from Taganga run to the Tayrona beaches and Cabo San Juan in calm months, which is a useful shortcut but weather-dependent and suspended in rough seas.

full.blurb: Colombia's most famous coastal park — jungle trails opening onto white-sand Caribbean coves like Cabo San Juan and Playa Cristal, about an hour east.

full.blurb: A long, laid-back backpacker beach town on the Caribbean about two hours east, known for river tubing and sunset surf.
full.name: Palomino

half.blurb: A cool mountain village in the Sierra Nevada foothills about 45 minutes inland, with coffee and cacao farms, the Pozo Azul and Marinka waterfalls, and superb birdwatching.
